title: Every day is a good day
hook: Yunmen asks about the days after the fifteenth, and answers himself: every day is a good day (Blue Cliff Record 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nanquan's cat, a hard one, and your line, sandals on the head. Today, something gentler.

Some days are plainly good. The test came back clear. The kids laughed at dinner. Someone you love said the thing you needed to hear. And some days are not. The car won't start. The news is bad. You say the wrong thing and lie awake replaying it. If someone told you on one of those days, every day is a good day, you might want to throw something at them. Yet in Japan those exact words can be found brushed in black ink on scrolls in tea rooms. They come from a Zen teacher who asked his monks a question no one could answer.
screen: `THE TEST CAME BACK CLEAR.` → `THE CAR WON'T START.` → `WORDS ON A SCROLL IN A TEA ROOM.`

segments.voice: The teacher was Yunmen, a Chan master of southern China, remembered for answers so short they land like a splash of cold water. The Blue Cliff Record, in case six, says he told his monks: I'm not asking you about the days before the fifteenth. Tell me something about the days after the fifteenth. Nobody said a word. So Yunmen answered for them: every day is a good day. The fifteenth is the middle of the lunar month, the night of the full moon. Teachers often read it as a picture: before the fifteenth is the time of practice and searching; after it is life after the moon is full, after insight. What's it like then? Every day is a good day. Here's what it doesn't mean. It doesn't mean every day is pleasant, or that you should paste a smile over grief. The good in Yunmen's line isn't the opposite of bad. It's more like: this day, exactly as it comes, is the one you get to live, and there's no better one waiting somewhere else. A day of loss is still a day of your life, and it can be met completely. Some teachers point out that a monk who says every day is a good day still weeps at a funeral. He just doesn't throw the day away. It sits close to the washed bowl from a few days back: Yunmen's line refuses to wait for some realer day. This one is it.
screen: `YUNMEN'S QUESTION.` · `AFTER THE FIFTEENTH.` · `NOT EVERY DAY IS PLEASANT.` · `NO BETTER DAY WAITING.` · then, large: `EVERY DAY IS A GOOD DAY.`

segments.voice: Look back over today so far, the whole thing, not just the highlights: the alarm, the first thing you ate, the small annoyance, the small kindness. Without grading any of it, let it all be today. Then look for one good thing hiding in it, even a tiny one, warm water, a sentence someone said, the fact that you're breathing now, and rest with that.
Yunmen. The Chan master who answered his own question about the days after the fifteenth with a four-word line: every day is a good day.
Your line: this one is it. Hard days are days of your life too. Two hundred eighty-six days now.

howItsDone: Yunmen's words are a familiar Zen phrase in Japan, where they're brushed as calligraphy and hung in tea rooms; teachers use the case to point to meeting each day fully rather than judging it.

original.note: Chinese rì rì shì hǎo rì; in Japanese, nichi nichi kore kōjitsu: every day is a good day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful slogan for looking on the bright side.
what it means: this day, exactly as it comes, is the one to live fully.
what a scholar hears: the 'fifteenth' is the full moon of the lunar month; Yunmen founded one of the five houses of Chan, and his line is case six of the Blue Cliff Record.
